f_conv_paper.text:
Conversation
Listen to a conversation on campus, then answer the questions.
f_conv_paper.say:
Student: Hi, Professor Grant. Do you have a minute? I wanted to talk about the research paper for your history class.
Professor: Of course, come in. What's on your mind?
Student: Well, I chose to write about the Silk Road, but I'm having trouble finding enough sources. Most of the books in the library are checked out.
Professor: That happens every semester with that topic. Have you tried the university's online database? It has digital copies of a lot of academic journals.
Student: Oh, I didn't know we had access to that.
Professor: You do. Just log in with your student ID. And if you're still stuck, you could narrow your topic. Maybe focus on how a single product, like paper or silk, spread along the route. That would require far fewer sources.
Student: That's a great idea. I think I'll focus on paper. Thanks!

f_conv_dorm.text:
Conversation
Listen to a conversation on campus, then answer the questions.
f_conv_dorm.say:
W: Hi, I live in Maple Hall, and I'd like to ask about moving to a different dorm next semester.
M: Sure. Is there a problem with your current room?
W: Not with the room itself. It's just that Maple Hall is on the far side of campus, and almost all my classes next semester are in the engineering building. It takes me twenty-five minutes to walk there.
M: I see. Well, Cedar Hall is right next to the engineering building, but it's usually full. You'd need to fill out a transfer request by November fifteenth, and rooms are assigned by lottery.
W: A lottery? So there's no guarantee.
M: Right. But if Cedar Hall doesn't work out, you could also consider getting a bike. The campus has bike lanes that go almost everywhere.

f_ann_lab.text:
Announcement
Listen to an announcement, then answer the questions.
f_ann_lab.say: Good afternoon, everyone. Before we begin today's lab, I have an important announcement. Starting next week, the chemistry building will be closed on Saturdays for safety inspections. That means the Saturday open lab hours are canceled for the rest of the month. If you need extra time to finish your experiments, the lab will now be open until nine p.m. on Tuesdays and Thursdays, instead of six. Also, please remember that safety goggles are required at all times. Anyone without goggles will be asked to leave the lab. No exceptions.

f_ann_career.text:
Announcement
Listen to an announcement, then answer the questions.
f_ann_career.say: Attention, students. The university's annual Career Fair will be held next Thursday from ten a.m. to four p.m. in the Student Union ballroom. More than sixty companies will be attending, including several from the technology and health care industries. To get the most out of the fair, we strongly recommend that you visit the Career Center beforehand to have your résumé reviewed. Walk-in hours are Monday through Wednesday, from one to five. And remember to dress professionally. Many employers will be conducting short interviews on the spot.

f_lec_bees.text:
Academic Talk
Listen to part of a lecture, then answer the questions.
f_lec_bees.say: Professor: Today I want to talk about how honeybees share information. When a forager bee finds a good source of nectar, it returns to the hive and performs what's called a waggle dance. The bee runs in a straight line while shaking its body from side to side, then circles back and repeats the movement. Now, here's what's remarkable. The direction of that straight run tells the other bees which way to fly. If the bee waggles straight up, toward the top of the honeycomb, that means: fly toward the sun. If it waggles at an angle, say, forty degrees to the right of vertical, the food is forty degrees to the right of the sun. And the length of the waggle run indicates distance. The longer the run, the farther away the food. Interestingly, researchers have found that bees adjust the angle of their dance over time, because the sun moves across the sky during the day. So the bees are, in a sense, keeping track of time.

f_lec_heat.text:
Academic Talk
Listen to part of a lecture, then answer the questions.
f_lec_heat.say:
Professor: Let's move on to something called the urban heat island effect. Cities are often several degrees warmer than the countryside around them, especially at night. Can anyone guess why?
Student: Is it because of all the cars and air conditioners?
Professor: That's part of it. Heat from vehicles and buildings does add up. But the bigger factor is the materials cities are made of. Asphalt and concrete absorb a lot of sunlight during the day and then slowly release that heat after the sun goes down. Rural areas, on the other hand, have more plants and soil. Plants release water vapor through their leaves, which cools the air, much like sweating cools your skin. So, what can cities do? Some have started painting rooftops white to reflect sunlight. Others are planting trees along streets or building rooftop gardens. In one study, neighborhoods with more trees were up to five degrees cooler on summer afternoons.

f_lec_paint.text:
Academic Talk
Listen to part of a lecture, then answer the questions.
f_lec_paint.say: Professor: When we think about why Impressionism developed in France in the 1870s, we usually talk about artists like Monet and Renoir wanting to capture light and everyday life. But there's a more practical factor that often gets overlooked: the paint tube. Before the 1840s, artists had to grind their own pigments and mix them with oil in the studio. The paint was often stored in pig bladders, which tended to burst and couldn't easily be carried around. Then, in 1841, an American painter named John Rand invented a collapsible metal tube that could be sealed with a cap. Suddenly, paint was portable. Artists could take their materials outdoors and paint directly in front of a landscape, which is exactly what the Impressionists became famous for. Renoir supposedly said that without paint in tubes, there would have been no Impressionism. Whether or not he really said it, the point stands: sometimes a simple technology can change the direction of art.

questions.q: Choose a Response — Listen to the speaker. Choose the best response.
options: Yes, it's open until two a.m. that week.
I returned the books last Friday.

questions.q: What is the professor's attitude toward the quote attributed to Renoir?

explain.text: supposedly、Whether or not he really said it＝不確定真的是他說的；the point stands＝但同意這個觀點。
